text: What is the pattern for a binary arithmetic operation in Rust?
expected_response: A binary arithmetic operation takes two parameters of the same type and returns the same type. The generic version uses the corresponding std::ops trait (Add, Sub, Mul, Div). Pattern: fn op(a: T, b: T) -> T where T implements the operation trait.

text: What is the pattern for a struct with methods in Rust?
expected_response: Define a struct with named fields, then implement methods in an impl block. Use &self for read-only methods, &mut self for mutations, and Self for constructors. Pattern: struct Name { fields } impl Name { fn new() -> Self, fn method(&self), fn mutate(&mut self) }.

text: What is the pattern for implementing a trait in Rust?
expected_response: Define a trait with method signatures, then implement it for specific types. This enables polymorphism — different types share a common interface. Pattern: trait Name { fn method(&self) -> ReturnType; } impl Name for ConcreteType { fn method(&self) -> ReturnType { ... } }.

text: What is the pattern for error handling with Result in Rust?
expected_response: Use Result<T, E> for operations that can fail. Define a custom error enum for the module. Use the ? operator to propagate errors. Pattern: define error type, return Result from functions, propagate with ?, handle at the boundary with match.

text: What is the pattern for an enum with data in Rust?
expected_response: Rust enums can carry data in each variant, making them algebraic data types. Use match to destructure. Pattern: enum Name { Variant1(Type), Variant2 { field: Type }, Variant3 } then match on all variants.

text: What is the pattern for iterators and method chaining in Rust?
expected_response: Rust iterators use method chaining: start with .iter() or .into_iter(), apply transformations (map, filter, flat_map), and collect the result. Lazy evaluation means no intermediate allocations. Pattern: collection.iter().filter(predicate).map(transform).collect().

text: What is the pattern for a recursive data structure in Rust?
expected_response: Recursive types require indirection via Box to give them a known size at compile time. Pattern: enum Node { Leaf(T), Branch(T, Box<Node>, Box<Node>) }. The Box provides heap allocation and a fixed-size pointer on the stack.

text: What is the pattern for Option handling in Rust?
expected_response: Option<T> represents a value that may or may not exist. Use map/and_then for chaining, unwrap_or for defaults, and if-let/match for control flow. Pattern: avoid unwrap(), chain with combinators, or use ? in functions returning Option.

text: What is the pattern for closures and higher-order functions in Rust?
expected_response: Closures capture their environment and can be passed as arguments. Higher-order functions take or return closures. Use Fn for read-only, FnMut for mutable, FnOnce for consuming closures. Pattern: fn apply<F: Fn(T) -> U>(f: F, val: T) -> U.

text: What is the pattern for async/await in Rust?
expected_response: Async functions return a Future that must be awaited or spawned on a runtime. Use async fn for the function, .await to suspend, and tokio or async-std as the runtime. Pattern: async fn fetch() -> Result<T, E> { let resp = client.get(url).await?; Ok(resp) }.

text: What is the pattern for implementing Display and Debug traits in Rust?
expected_response: Display is for user-facing output (used by {} in format strings), Debug is for developer output (used by {:?}). Derive Debug automatically, implement Display manually. Pattern: #[derive(Debug)] for the struct, impl fmt::Display for Name { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result }.

text: What is the pattern for lifetime annotations in Rust?
expected_response: Lifetimes tell the compiler how long references are valid, preventing dangling references. Most are inferred (elision rules). Explicit lifetimes needed when a function returns a reference that could come from multiple inputs. Pattern: fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str — the output lives as long as both inputs.

text: What is the pattern for lifetime annotations in Rust?
expected_response: Lifetime annotations tell the compiler how long references are valid. Use them on function signatures when the return borrows from an input, on structs that hold references, and on impl blocks. The compiler enforces that the borrowed data outlives the reference.

Rust has three lifetime elision rules that let you omit explicit annotations in common cases: (1) each input reference gets its own lifetime, (2) if there is exactly one input lifetime it is assigned to all outputs, (3) if one input is &self or &mut self its lifetime is assigned to all outputs.

text: How do lifetime annotations work in Rust structs and functions?
expected_response: Lifetime annotations on structs ensure the struct cannot outlive the data it borrows. On functions, they express the relationship between input and output reference lifetimes. Use 'static for references that live for the entire program.

text: What is the pattern for async/await in Rust?
expected_response: In Rust, async fn returns a Future that must be awaited or spawned on a runtime (like tokio). Use .await to suspend until the future completes. Pin the future if it borrows across await points. Use tokio::spawn for concurrent tasks and tokio::select! for racing futures.

text: How does async/await work in Rust with tokio?
expected_response: Rust async functions return a Future that does nothing until polled. The tokio runtime polls futures cooperatively. Use .await to yield control back to the runtime. tokio::spawn runs tasks concurrently. tokio::select! races multiple futures.

text: Explain the async/await pattern and futures in Rust
expected_response: A Future in Rust is a lazy computation that produces a value when polled to completion. The async keyword transforms a function body into a state machine implementing Future. The .await keyword yields control until the inner future resolves. An executor (like tokio) drives futures to completion by polling them.
